stimulus.title: Why Do Leaves Change Colour?
stimulus.body: Every autumn, forests across southern Australia put on a quiet but spectacular display as certain deciduous trees shift from green to gold, orange and deep red. Because chlorophyll production increases during this period, requiring extra protection.
Because the tree is attracting insects to help spread its seeds before winter.

questions.explanation: The passage links the new red pigment directly to a protective purpose, 'a defence against sunlight damage while the tree withdraws its remaining nutrients.' stimulus.title: The Beekeeper's Warning
stimulus.body: Nadia had visited her grandfather's orchard every summer since she could walk, but she had never been allowed near the beehives until this year. 'Bees are not our enemies,' her grandfather said, tightening the strap on her borrowed veil, 'but they are diplomats, not pushovers. Move like a shadow, and they will forgive almost anything.' As they approached the first hive, she noticed her grandfather's steps slow to an almost theatrical crawl, his breathing low and even. options.text: It suggests her nervousness felt sharp, buzzing and slightly dangerous, echoing the bees she was about to face.
It shows that Nadia had accidentally disturbed a real nest of hornets earlier that day.
It proves that Nadia was more frightened of hornets than of bees.
It explains why her grandfather decided she was not ready to visit the hives.

questions.explanation: The comparison to a 'nest of hornets' is figurative, not literal, since nothing in the text suggests a real hornet encounter. A plainer word such as 'nervous' would have described her feeling accurately, but would not have connected it to the world of stinging insects she is about to enter. Choosing hornets instead lets the author echo the danger and buzz of the bees themselves, making Nadia's anxiety feel sharper and more physical. This kind of figurative choice deliberately links a character's inner feeling to the story's central subject, deepening the reader's sense of tension.

questions.prompt: What can readers infer about Nadia's experience with beehives before the events of this passage?

stimulus.title: The Beekeeper's Warning
stimulus.body: Nadia had visited her grandfather's orchard every summer since she could walk, but she had never been allowed near the beehives until this year. 'Bees are not our enemies,' her grandfather said, tightening the strap on her borrowed veil, 'but they are diplomats, not pushovers. Move like a shadow, and they will forgive almost anything.' Nadia laughed nervously, though her stomach had turned into a nest of hornets itself. As they approached the first hive, she noticed her grandfather's steps slow to an almost theatrical crawl, his breathing low and even. A single bee landed on her sleeve and simply sat there, as if deciding whether she was worth the trouble of a sting. Nadia held perfectly still, remembering his warning, and after a long moment the bee lifted off and drifted back towards the hive entrance without incident.

options.text: She had never been close to the hives before this visit.
She had helped her grandfather manage the hives for many years.
She was more experienced with bees than her grandfather was.
She had been stung by bees several times in the past.

questions.explanation: The passage states directly that Nadia 'had never been allowed near the beehives until this year,' which tells readers she lacked prior close experience with them. This is true even though she had visited the orchard itself for many summers, since visiting an orchard is not the same as being allowed near its hives. Nothing in the passage suggests she had helped manage the hives, been stung previously, or was more experienced than her grandfather. Only the first option is directly supported by the passage's own wording about this being her first time near the hives.

questions.prompt: Maria completely and carelessly forgot to pack her favourite umbrella before hurriedly leaving for school that particular drizzly morning; ___, she was thoroughly soaked from head to toe by the time she finally reached the crowded, sheltered bus stop. , she was soaked by the time she reached the bus stop.

questions.explanation: Forgetting the umbrella is the direct cause of Maria getting soaked on her way to school, so a cause-and-effect connective is required here. Words such as 'as a result', 'consequently', 'therefore' or 'so' correctly link the two clauses, showing that the second event follows logically from the first. A contrast connective such as 'however' would not make sense here, since nothing in the sentence suggests an unexpected or opposing outcome. An addition connective such as 'also' would likewise fail to capture the causal relationship the sentence describes.
